cues.text: ODYSSEY — BOOK XVI
Father and son: the recognition at the swineherd's hut.
But the two in the hut, Odysseus and the noble swineherd,
had lit a fire and were readying breakfast at dawn,\nand had sent the herdsmen out with the gathered swine;
and around Telemachus the yapping dogs went fawning,\nand did not bark as he came. And noble Odysseus noticed
the dogs fawning, and the sound of footsteps came to him.
At once he spoke winged words to Eumaeus:
"Eumaeus, surely some companion of yours is coming,
or another man well known, since the dogs are not barking\nbut fawn around him; and I hear the thud of feet."
The word was not all spoken when his own dear son\nstood in the gateway. The swineherd sprang up amazed,
and out of his hands fell the vessels he was busy with,
mixing the sparkling wine. He went to meet his master,\nand kissed his head, and both his beautiful eyes,
and both his hands; and a warm tear fell from him.
And as a father, in the fullness of his heart,\nembraces his son come from a far country in the tenth year,
an only son, late-born,\nfor whom he has suffered many sorrows —
so then the noble swineherd took godlike Telemachus
in his arms and kissed him all over, as one escaped\nfrom death; and sobbing he spoke winged words to him:
"You have come, Telemachus — sweet light! I told myself
I would never see you again,\nonce you had gone by ship to Pylos.
Come in now, come, dear child, so my heart may take\nits joy of looking at you, newly here from elsewhere.
You do not often visit the farm and the herdsmen;
you stay in town: so, it seems, it has pleased your heart —\nto look on that deadly crowd of the suitor-men."
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered him:
"So be it, old father.\nIt is for your sake I have come here,
to see you with my eyes, and to hear you tell me\nwhether my mother still remains in the halls, or by now
some other man has married her, and Odysseus' bed lies\nempty of sleepers, holding only foul spider-webs."
Then the swineherd answered him, a leader of men:
"Indeed she remains, with an enduring heart,\nin your own halls; and always in misery
her nights and her days waste away in weeping."
So speaking, he took the bronze spear from him,\nand Telemachus went in and crossed the stone threshold.
As he came on, his father Odysseus yielded his seat;\nbut Telemachus, from his side, checked him and said:
"Sit, stranger. We will find a seat elsewhere in our\nown farmstead. Here is the man who will set one."
So he spoke; and Odysseus went back\nand sat down. And the swineherd
strewed green brushwood under, and a fleece on top,\nand there the dear son of Odysseus seated himself.
And the swineherd set before them platters of roasted
meat, which they had left from their eating the day\nbefore, and briskly heaped up bread in the baskets,
and mixed honey-sweet wine in an ivy-wood bowl,\nand himself sat down opposite godlike Odysseus.
And their hands went out to the\ngood things spread before them.
But when they had put away desire for food and drink,\nthen Telemachus spoke to the noble swineherd:
"Old father, where has this guest\nof yours come from? How did sailors
bring him to Ithaca? Who did they claim to be?
For I hardly think he came here on foot."
And you answered him, Eumaeus the swineherd:
"Then I will tell you, child, the whole truth of it.
He claims his birth from Crete\nof the wide dancing-grounds,
and says he has wandered rolling through many\ncities of mortal men: so a god has spun it for him.
Now, run off from a ship of Thesprotian men,\nhe has come to my farmstead; and I put him in your hands.
Do as you will. He declares himself your suppliant."
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered him:
"Eumaeus, this word of yours cuts to the heart.
How am I to receive this guest in my house?
I am young myself, and have no faith yet in my hands\nto defend a man, when someone picks a quarrel first.
And my mother's heart is divided in her breast, two ways:
whether to stay here with me and keep the house,\nrespecting her husband's bed and the voice of the people,
or to follow now whichever of the Achaeans is best\namong her suitors in the halls, and offers the most.
But as for this guest, since he has come to your house,
I will dress him in a cloak and a tunic, fine clothing,
and give him a two-edged sword, and sandals for his feet,
and send him wherever his heart and spirit bid him go.
Or if you will, keep him and care for him at the farmstead,\nand I will send clothing here, and all his bread
to eat, so he will not wear you down, you and your men.
But in among the suitors I would not let him go:\ntoo reckless is the insolence they carry —
they would mock him,\nand it would be a terrible grief to me.
It is hard for one man to get anything done among many,\neven a strong man: they are far the more powerful."
Then much-enduring noble Odysseus spoke to him:
"Friend — since surely it is right for me to answer\nalso — truly my heart is eaten through as I listen,
hearing you tell what reckless things the suitors
devise in the halls, against\nthe will of such a man as you.
Tell me: do you bow to it willingly, or do the people
through the land hate you, following the voice of a god?
Or have you some fault to find with brothers — those a man
trusts to fight beside him, though a great feud rise?
Ah, would that I were as young as this anger of mine,
or were a son of blameless Odysseus, or the man himself —
then straightway might some\nstranger cut the head from my neck
if I did not walk into the hall of Laertes' son\nOdysseus, and become an evil to every man of them.
And if they overpowered me by their numbers,\nalone as I am, I would rather die cut down in my own halls
than look on forever at these disgraceful doings:
guests roughly handled, and men hauling the\nslave-women shamefully through the beautiful house,
and wine drawn off and squandered,\nand them eating my bread
idly, recklessly, endlessly —\nfor a work never to be finished."
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered him:
"Then I will tell you, stranger, exactly how it is.
It is not that the whole people\nhates me and bears a grudge,
nor have I fault to find with brothers — those a man\ntrusts to fight beside him, though a great feud rise.
For so the son of Cronos has\nmade ours a line of only sons:
Arceisius fathered Laertes, an only son;\nhis father got Odysseus, an only son; and Odysseus
fathered only me, and left me in\nthe halls, and had no joy of me.
And that is why enemies past counting are in the house.
All the great men who hold power among the islands —\nDulichium and Same and wooded Zacynthus —
and all who lord it through rocky Ithaca:
so many woo my mother, and wear this house away.
And she neither refuses the marriage she loathes,\nnor can she bring it to an end. And they eat on, wasting
my house. Soon they will tear me to pieces too.
But surely these things lie on the knees of the gods.
Old father, you go — quickly —\nand tell steady-hearted Penelope
that I am safe for her, and have come back from Pylos.
I will stay here. And you return to this place
when you have told her — her only.\nLet none of the other Achaeans
learn it: for there are many devising evil against me."
And you answered him, Eumaeus the swineherd:
"I know. I understand.\nYou order a man who is thinking it too.
But come, tell me this, and tell it to me truly:
shall I go the same road with the news to Laertes
as well? Poor man — for a long\nwhile, for all his great grief
for Odysseus, he still would oversee\nthe field-works, and in the house
would drink and eat with the slaves,\nwhenever the heart within him bade.
But now, from the day you went by ship to Pylos,\nthey say he no longer eats and drinks as before,
nor looks to the field-works,\nbut with moaning and groaning
sits mourning; and the flesh\nwastes away around his bones."
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered him:
"The harder for it; but all the same we\nwill let him be, though it grieves us.
For if everything whatever could\nbe had for the choosing by mortals,
we would choose first the day of my father's homecoming.
No — give your message and come back; do not go\nwandering over the fields after him. But tell my mother
to send her handmaid, the housekeeper, quickly —\nand secretly: she could carry the news to the old man."
He spoke, and roused the swineherd,\nwho took his sandals in his hands,
bound them under his feet, and set off for the city.
Escape Athena, that Eumaeus the\nswineherd was gone from the farm:
she came near; and in body she was like a woman\nbeautiful and tall, and skilled in glorious handwork.
She stood at the door of the hut,\nshowing herself to Odysseus;
but Telemachus did not see her\nbefore him, did not sense her —
for the gods do not appear manifest to everyone —\nbut Odysseus saw her, and the dogs: and they did not bark,
but whimpered and shrank in fear\nto the far side of the farmstead.
She signaled with her brows;\nand noble Odysseus understood,
and came out of the hall, past the great wall of the yard,\nand stood before her; and Athena said to him:
"Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus of the many devices:
now speak your word to your son. Hide it no longer —\nso that you two may fit death and doom to the suitors
and go to the famous city. And I myself will not\nbe long away from you: I am hungry for battle."
She spoke, and Athena touched him with her golden wand.
First she laid a well-washed mantle and a tunic about\nhis chest, and filled out his frame and his youth:
dark color came back to his skin, his jaws grew full,\nand the beard about his chin turned blue-black again.
That done, she went away again; and Odysseus went\ninto the hut. His dear son was struck with wonder,
and turned his eyes aside, afraid, in case it was a god,\nand lifting his voice he spoke winged words to him:
"Stranger, you look other to me now than a moment ago:
you wear other clothes; your skin is not the same.
Surely you are some god,\none of those who hold wide heaven.
Be gracious, then! — and we will give you pleasing\nsacrifices, and wrought gifts of gold. Only spare us."
Then much-enduring noble Odysseus answered him:
"I am no god. Why do you liken me to the immortals?
No: I am your father — for whose sake you go groaning
and suffer many pains,\nand take men's violence on yourself."
So speaking, he kissed his son, and down his cheeks
a tear fell to the ground. Before,\nhe had held them back, always.
But Telemachus — for he did not\nyet believe it was his father —
found words again, and said to him in answer:
"You are not Odysseus, not my father. A god is casting\na spell on me, so I may sob and grieve still more.
No mortal man could ever contrive these things\nby his own wit — not unless a god in person came
and made him young or old at a stroke, at will.
Just now, I know, you were old, and meanly dressed;\nand now you are like the gods who hold wide heaven."
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered him:
"Telemachus, it is not right, when your own father is here,\nto marvel at him past measure, or stand amazed.
No other Odysseus will ever come to you here:
he is I — such as you see,\nhaving suffered, having wandered long —
come in the twentieth year to my father's land.
But this — this is the work of\nAthena, driver of the spoil,
who makes of me whatever she wills — for she has\nthe power — now like a beggar man, and now again
like a young man with fine clothes upon his body.
It is easy for the gods who hold wide heaven\nto glorify a mortal man — or to break him."
So speaking he sat down; and Telemachus, flinging his\narms around his noble father, wept and shed tears,
and in both of them rose the longing for lament.
They cried shrill, in bursts\nthicker than the cries of birds —
of ospreys, or of vultures with\ncrooked talons, whose young
the country people have taken from\nthe nest before they were fledged:
so pitifully the tears fell from beneath their brows.
And the light of the sun would\nhave gone down on their weeping
had not Telemachus suddenly spoken to his father:
"What ship was it, dear father,\nwhose sailors brought you here to Ithaca?
For I hardly think you came here on foot."
Then much-enduring noble Odysseus spoke to him:
"Then I will tell you, child, the truth of it.
The Phaeacians brought me, famed for their ships,\nwho give passage to other men too, whoever comes to them.
They carried me asleep in a fast ship over the sea\nand set me down in Ithaca, and gave me shining gifts,
bronze and gold in plenty, and woven clothing —\nall lying now in caves, by the gods' will.
And I have come here at Athena's prompting,\nso we may plan together the slaughter of our enemies.
Come, count me off the suitors, one by one,\nso I may know how many they are, and what men;
then I will weigh it in my blameless heart, and decide\nwhether we two can stand against them by ourselves,
alone, or should look for others."
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered him:
"Father, I have always heard your great fame:
a spearman with your hands, and weighty in counsel.
But what you say is too great.\nAwe holds me. It could not be
for two men to fight with many, and strong men too.
The suitors are no exact ten, nor two tens only,\nbut many more. You shall have the count here and now.
From Dulichium, two-and-fifty young men,\nchosen, and six serving-men follow with them;
from Same there are four-and-twenty men;\nfrom Zacynthus, twenty young Achaeans;
and from Ithaca itself, twelve, all of them the best;
and with them are Medon the herald,\nand the godlike singer,
and two henchmen skilled in the carving of meats.
If we come against all of these inside the house,
beware: your avenging of their violence\ncould cost too bitter, too grim a price.
No — you, if you can think of some defender, think of\none who would stand by us two with a willing heart."
Then much-enduring noble Odysseus answered him:
"Then I will tell you — mark me now, and listen.
Consider: will Athena, with father Zeus beside her,
be enough for us two? Or shall\nI think of some other defender?"
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered him:
"Good defenders indeed, those two you name,\nthough they sit high among the clouds; and they rule
all others — men in their power, and the deathless gods."
Then much-enduring noble Odysseus answered him:
"Those two will not stand long apart from the strong\ndin of battle, when between the suitors and ourselves
the war-strength of Ares is put to trial in my halls.
But you, for now: go home at the showing of\nthe dawn and mix among the overweening suitors;
and later the swineherd will bring me to the city,\nlooking like a beggar, wretched and old.
And if they treat me shamefully in the house,\nlet the heart in your breast endure it while I suffer —
even if they drag me by the feet\nthrough the hall to the door,
or throw things and hit me: look on, and hold yourself in.
Tell them, yes, to stop their follies —\nwin at them with gentle words. They will not listen,
not at all: for their fated day is standing near.
Lay it up in your heart.
When Athena of the many counsels puts it in my mind,\nI will nod to you with my head; and when you see it,
take all the weapons of war that lie about the hall\nand store them up in the corner of the high chamber —
all of them; and when the suitors miss them\nand ask you, talk them around with soft words:
'I laid them out of the smoke:\nthey no longer looked like the arms
Odysseus left behind when he went to Troy — they are\nfouled over, as far as the breath of the fire reached.
And a greater fear the son of Cronos put into my heart:
that in your wine you might raise a quarrel among\nyou and wound one another, and shame the feast
and the wooing. For iron of itself draws a man on.'
But for us two alone leave out two swords, two spears,\nand two oxhide shields for our hands to seize,
so we can rush and take them up; and the suitors —\nPallas Athena and Zeus the counselor will daze them.
And another thing I will tell you:\nlay it up in your heart.
If you are truly mine, and truly of our blood,\nthen let no one hear that Odysseus is within —
not Laertes: he is not to know it; nor the swineherd,\nnor any of the household; no — not Penelope herself.
You and I alone will learn the set of the women;\nand we might test this or that man of the slaves as well:
where one honors the two of us, and fears us in his heart,
and where one cares nothing,\nand slights you — such as you are."
Then his shining son spoke out, answered him:
"Father — you will come to know my heart hereafter,\nI think; there is no slackness in me — none.
But I do not believe this plan will be a\nprofit to us both. Think again, I urge you.
You will be a long time going round the farms and testing
each man, one by one;\nand meanwhile in the halls, at their ease,
they eat through our goods with\na high hand, and spare nothing.
The women — yes, I would have you find out which\nones dishonor you, and which are guiltless.
But the men about the farmsteads — I for one would\nrather we not test them now. Keep that work for later,
if you truly know some sign\nfrom Zeus who bears the aegis."
So they spoke to each other of such things.
And meanwhile the well-built\nship was putting in to Ithaca,
the ship that carried Telemachus\nfrom Pylos with all his companions.
When they had come inside the deep harbor,\nthey hauled the black ship up onto the land,
and high-spirited henchmen carried off their gear and\ntook the beautiful gifts straight to Clytius' house.
And they sent a herald ahead to the house of Odysseus\nto bring the news to watchful-minded Penelope —
that Telemachus was in the country, and had ordered\nthe ship to sail on to the city — lest the strong queen
take fright at heart, and let the soft tear fall.
And the two of them met,\nthe herald and the noble swineherd,
come on the same errand, to bring the woman word.
But when they reached the house of the godlike king,\nthe herald spoke out in the midst of the slave-women:
"Already, O queen, your dear son has come home."
But the swineherd stood close to Penelope and told\nher everything her dear son had charged him to say.
And when he had delivered the whole of his commission,
he went his way to his swine,\nand left the walls and the hall.
But the suitors were downcast, dejected in spirit,\nand came out of the hall past the great wall of the yard,
and there before the gates they sat themselves down.
And Eurymachus, Polybus' son, began to speak among them:
"Friends, here is a great work brought off insolently —
this voyage of Telemachus.\nWe swore it would never be done.
Come — let us drag down a black ship, the best we have,\nand gather seamen for rowers, to carry word
quickly to those two out there: come home at speed."
He had not finished speaking when Amphinomus,\nturning in his place, saw the ship inside the deep harbor,
the crew furling the sail and\nholding the oars in their hands.
He broke into easy laughter and called to his companions:
"No need now to send any message. They are in.
Either some god told them, or they saw the ship\nthemselves passing by — and could not catch her."
So he spoke; and they rose and\nwent to the shore of the sea.
Quickly the men hauled the black ship up onto the land,\nand high-spirited henchmen carried off their gear;
and they themselves went in a body\nto the assembly-place, and allowed
no one else to sit among them, young or old.
And Antinous spoke among them, Eupeithes' son:
"Damn it all — see how the gods have\nslipped this man out of harm's reach!
Day after day our watchers sat on the windy headlands,
relief upon relief of them; and with the sun gone down\nwe never passed a night ashore, but afloat on the sea
in our fast ship we waited for the bright Dawn,\nlying in ambush for Telemachus, to take him
and kill him. And all the while\nsome god has brought him home.
Then let us here devise a wretched death
for Telemachus — not let him slip\nbetween our hands. For I tell you,
while he lives, this business\nof ours will not be brought off.
In counsel and in mind, and the people\nno longer look on us with any favor.
Act, then — before he can call the Achaeans together\nto assembly. He will not hang back, I promise you:
he will keep his anger; he will\nstand up among them all and tell
how we wove sheer murder for him —\nand could not catch him.
And they will not praise us, hearing of evil deeds.
Beware they do not do us harm, and drive us out of\nour own country, and we come to the land of strangers.
Take him first: catch him in the field, far from the city,
or on the road. His livelihood\nand goods we hold ourselves,
dividing them share and share among us; the house
we would give his mother to keep —\nhers and the man who weds her.
But if this word displeases you, and you choose instead\nthat he live, and keep all that was his father's —
then let us not go on gathering here to eat away
his store of pleasant things.\nLet each man from his own hall
court her with bride-gifts, seeking her; and she then
may wed the man who gives the most,\nand comes as her fate."
So he spoke; and they all fell silent and still.
Then Amphinomus rose and spoke among them —\nthe shining son of Nisus, of the lord Aretias' line,
who from Dulichium, land of wheat and grass,\nled the suitors; and beyond the others he pleased
Penelope with his talk, for his mind was set on good.
With good intent he rose and spoke among them:
"Friends, I for one would have no wish to kill Telemachus.\nDreadful it is to kill the blood of kings.
No — first let us ask what is the counsel of the gods.
If the ordinances of great Zeus approve it,\nI will kill him myself, and bid all the rest to help;
but if the gods turn us aside, I say: stop here."
So spoke Amphinomus, and his word pleased them well.
They rose at once and went to the house of Odysseus,\nand coming in they sat on the polished chairs.
Then watchful-minded Penelope thought of one thing more:
to show herself to the suitors\nin their overweening insolence.
For she had learned of her son's\ndeath plotted in the halls —
the herald Medon told her,\nwho had overheard their counsels.
She went down to the hall with her attendant women.
And when she reached the suitors, shining among women,\nshe stood beside the pillar of the close-built roof,
holding her glistening veil before her cheeks,\nand rebuked Antinous, and spoke a word, and named him:
"Antinous — insolence itself,\ndeviser of evils! And they say
that in the land of Ithaca you are the best of your years
in counsel and in speech. You were never such a man.
Madman! Why do you weave death and doom for Telemachus,\nand pay no heed to suppliants — over whom
Zeus stands witness? It is unholy\nto weave evil against each other.
Do you not know the day your father came here in flight,
in terror of the people? For they were bitterly enraged,\nbecause he had joined with Taphian pirates
to harry the Thesprotians — men who were our allies.
They wanted to destroy him,\nto tear the dear heart out of him,
and to swallow his great and pleasing livelihood whole;
but Odysseus held them back and\nchecked them, hot as they were.
His house you now eat up scot-free; you woo his wife;\nyou would kill his son; and me you grieve to the core.
Stop, I command you. And command the rest to stop."
Then Eurymachus, Polybus' son, answered her:
"Daughter of Icarius, watchful-minded Penelope,\ntake heart. Do not let these things trouble your mind.
The man does not exist, will not exist, cannot be\nborn who shall lay hands upon your son Telemachus
while I am alive and look upon the light of the earth.
For I will say this outright, and it will be accomplished:
in an instant his black blood would run down my spear —
that man's. For Odysseus, sacker of cities —\nmany a time he sat me on his knees, and put roast meat
into my hands, and held the red wine to my lips.
And so Telemachus is to me by far the dearest of all men;\nand I tell him he need not tremble at death —
not from the suitors. From the gods there is no escaping."
So he spoke to soothe her — and was\nhimself preparing the boy's destruction.
But she climbed to her shining upper room,\nand wept there for Odysseus, her dear husband, until
gray-eyed Athena cast sweet sleep upon her eyelids.
And at evening the noble swineherd came back to\nOdysseus and his son. They were making their supper,
busy about it, having killed a year-old pig.\nBut Athena came and stood close by Laertes' son Odysseus,
and struck him with her wand\nand made him an old man again,
and dressed his body in miserable\nclothes — lest the swineherd
look at him face to face and\nknow him, and go with the news
to steady-hearted Penelope,\nnot holding it fast in his heart.
And Telemachus was first to speak to him:
"You have come, noble Eumaeus. What news in the town?
Are the haughty suitors back inside by now, home from\ntheir ambush — or still watching for me on my way?"
And you answered him, Eumaeus the swineherd:
"I had no mind to ask about that, going down\nthrough the town. My heart said: tell your message
and be quick, and come back here again.
And a swift messenger from your companions overtook me,\na herald — and he spoke to your mother first.
But this much more I know; this I saw with my eyes.
I was already above the city, where the hill of Hermes\nstands, on my way, when I saw a fast ship coming down
into our harbor. There were many men aboard her,\nand she rode heavy with shields and double-pointed spears.
I thought it was they — but I cannot know."
So he spoke; and the sacred strength of Telemachus smiled,
and his eyes went to his father —\nslipping past the swineherd's.
And when they had ceased their\nlabor and made the meal ready,
they feasted; and no man's appetite\nwent short of the equal feast.
But when they had put away desire for food and drink,
they remembered their beds, and took the gift of sleep.
